text: The 2004 African Cup of Nations final was a football match played on 14 February 2004 between Tunisia and Morocco at the 7 November Stadium in Tunis, Tunisia. It determined the winner of the 24th edition of the biennial African tournament organized by the Confederation of African Football (CAF). Morocco qualified for the final for the first time in their history, while Tunisia reached the final for the third time. Tunisia won the match in regulation time with a score of 2–1, securing their first Africa Cup of Nations title, while Morocco finished in second place. Tunisia took the lead in the 5th minute with a goal from Francileudo Santos, but Morocco responded with a goal from Youssef Mokhtari in the 38th minute before Ziad Jaziri restored Tunisia's lead in the 52nd minute. The African Cup of Nations, organized by CAF, is the primary international association football competition for African national teams, with the 2004 tournament being its 24th edition since its inception. This was the first time the two teams faced each other in the final, having previously met twice in the group stage in 1978 and 2000. Tunisia had not won the title before 2004, having lost the final in 1965 on home soil to Ghana 2–3 after extra time and again in 1996 in South Africa 0–2. Morocco had won the title once, in 1976 in Ethiopia. The 7 November Stadium, located in Radès, about 10 kilometers south-east of Tunis city center, is a multi-purpose stadium with a capacity of 60,000 and was built in 2001 for the 2001 Mediterranean Games. It features a covered area of 13,000 m², including a central area, three adjoining grounds, two warm-up rooms, two paintings, and an official stand of 7,000 seats, with a press gallery equipped with 300 desks. Tunisia entered the tournament for the 11th time as hosts and was one of the favorites, having never won the title before, with two prior final appearances. In the opening Group A match at the stadium, Tunisia defeated Rwanda 2–1, with Ziad Jaziri scoring in the 27th minute, João Elias Manamana equalizing in the 31st minute, and Francileudo Santos scoring in the 57th minute. In the second match against DR Congo, Tunisia won 3–0 after Lomana LuaLua received a red card, with Santos scoring in the 55th minute, Najeh Braham in the 65th, and Santos again in the 87th. In the match against Guinea, Tunisia drew 1–1 after Selim Benachour scored in the 85th minute and Titi Camara equalized late. Tunisia topped Group A with seven points from two wins and a draw and advanced to the quarter-finals. In the quarter-final against Senegal, Tunisia won 1–0 with a header from Jawhar Mnari via a scissor pass from Jaziri in the 65th minute. In the semi-final against Nigeria, the match ended 1–1 after Jay-Jay Okocha scored a penalty in the 67th minute and Khaled Badra equalized with a penalty in the 87th minute, with Tunisia winning 5–3 in penalties, including Ali Boumnijel saving Peter Odemwingie’s spot-kick and Tunisians converting all five of their penalties. Morocco entered the tournament for the 12th time, previously winning in 1976 in Ethiopia after topping their group and drawing their final match against Guinea 1–1. In Group D, Morocco beat Nigeria 1–0 with Youssef Hadji scoring in the 77th minute, defeated Benin 4–0 with Marouane Chamakh scoring in the 17th minute, an own goal by Anicet Adjamossi in the 73rd minute, Abdeslam Ouaddou in the 75th, and Talal El Karkouri in the 80th, and drew 1–1 with South Africa after Patrick Mayo scored in the first half and Youssef Safri equalized with a penalty eight minutes later. Morocco topped Group D with seven points from two wins and a draw and advanced to the quarter-finals. In the quarter-final against Algeria, the match ended in a draw after Abdelmalek Cherrad scored in the 84th minute, Chamakh equalized in stoppage time, Hadji scored in the 113th minute, and Jawad Zairi added a goal in the 120+1 minute, resulting in a 3–1 victory for Morocco. In the semi-final against Mali, Youssef Mokhtari opened the scoring in the 15th minute and doubled it in the 58th, Hadji scored in the 80th, and Nabil Baha sealed the win in the 90+1 minute, sending Morocco to the final for the first time. The final was officiated by Senegalese referee Falla N'Doye, assisted by Ali Tomusange of Uganda and Brighton Mudzamiri of Zimbabwe, with Coffi Codjia of Benin as the fourth official. N'Doye, who became an international referee in 1995 and officiated one match at the 2002 FIFA World Cup, had previously refereed matches between Rwanda and DR Congo and Nigeria and Morocco during the tournament. This was the second time a Senegalese referee had overseen an Africa Cup of Nations final, following Badara Sène in 1992. Key figures attending the match included President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and his wife Leïla Ben Ali, FIFA President Sepp Blatter, CAF President Issa Hayatou, and AFC President Mohamed Bin Hammam. The final, held in front of 60,000 supporters, began with Tunisia taking a 1–0 lead in the fourth minute when Mehdi Nafti centered to Francileudo Santos, who scored his fourth goal of the tournament. At the end of the first half, Morocco equalized through Youssouf Hadji on a pass from Youssef Mokhtari. Seven minutes into the second half, Jaziri scored again to give Tunisia the lead. The match ended 2–1, giving Tunisia their first Africa Cup of Nations title. After the final whistle, jubilation erupted, with Tunisian players performing a circuit of the pitch and climbing onto the podium to receive gold medals, while Moroccan players received silver medals. President Ben Ali presented the trophy to Khaled Badra and Riadh Bouazizi, who raised it high. The Super Eagles of Carthage became the 13th national team in history to win the African championship, and Roger Lemerre became the first coach to win two different continental tournaments after previously winning Euro 2000 with France. On 24 February, President Ben Ali received the Tunisian team at the Carthage Palace, accompanied by technical and administrative staff, and awarded them the National Order of Merit. Tunisia also won the African National Team of the Year award from CAF. The two teams faced each other again in Group 5 during the second round of the 2006 FIFA World Cup qualification, with the first leg in Rabat ending 1–1 and the second leg in Tunis ending 2–2, with Tunisia securing its fourth World Cup qualification by finishing top of the group, while Morocco failed to qualify, finishing one point behind.
